Vaud
voh
n. (the Pays de Vaud, conquered by Bern from Savoy in 1536 and reformed by the Lausanne disputation, where Calvin first spoke in public)
French Vaud, from the Germanic Wald, a forest, through Latin Waldensis pagus; the Pays de Vaud lies along the north shore of Lake Geneva.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Vaud is the French-speaking country that Bern took by arms and reformed by argument. Savoy had held it; Bern conquered it in the winter and spring of 1536 and, instead of simply decreeing the Reformation, summoned a public disputation at Lausanne for the first week of October 1536, where William Farel and Pierre Viret led the Reformed side against the clergy of the diocese and the doctors of the Sorbonne's party. It was at Lausanne that a young Frenchman lately arrived in Geneva, John Calvin, rose and answered a charge that the Reformed despised the fathers by citing Tertullian, Chrysostom and Augustine from memory at length, which was his first public appearance in the Swiss Reformation. The disputation concluded for the Reformed, the mass was abolished across the Pays, and Bern founded the academy at Lausanne in 1537, where Viret and Theodore Beza taught. It ended badly: Viret and his colleagues held that a congregation must be able to exclude the scandalous from the Supper, Bern held that discipline belonged to its own council, and in 1559 Bern expelled them. They went to Geneva, and Beza became the first rector of Calvin's academy there. The dictionary enters Vaud because Bern's refusal of church discipline furnished Geneva with its best man.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a disputation as a contest by arguments; an academy as a school of learning; excommunication as the act of ejecting from communion; and a rector as the head of a school.

expand to see more

DISPUTATION, n. A contest in words or by arguments; a public exercise in argumentation, as before a council.

ACADEMY, n. A school or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school.

EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from the communion of the faithful.

RECTOR, n. The chief elective officer of some universities; the master of a school.

CONQUEST, n. The act of conquering; the subjection of a country or people by arms.

Key Scripture

1Co 5:13 — "But them that are without God judgeth. Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person."

Mat 18:17 — "And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican."

1Co 11:28 — "But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup."

Act 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Modern Corruption

French-speaking country taken by Bern from Savoy in 1536 and reformed by the Lausanne disputation, whose ministers Bern expelled in 1559 over church discipline.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the magistrate's seizure of the keys, and Vaud is where it cost the most. Bern's doctrine was Reformed and its council was pious, and it held that admission to and exclusion from the Lord's table was a civil administrative matter. The Lord gave that judgement to the congregation: “tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican” (Mat 18:17), and the apostolic command over a scandalous member is addressed to the body, “Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (1Co 5:13).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the self-examination and the oversight that together guard the table. The communicant is told “let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread” (1Co 11:28), and the officers are charged by the Holy Ghost to “feed the church of God” (Act 20:28). Bern took the second half into its own hands and lost Viret and Beza in 1559 for it, and the dictionary notes the irony without pretending it was providence excusing Bern: Geneva's academy opened because Lausanne's teachers were turned out.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ekklesia (G1577), the assembly; Greek exairo (G1808), to put away; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to examine, to prove.

expand to see more

Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out, the church; “tell it unto the church”, Matthew 18:17.

Greek telones (G5057) — a tax-gatherer, a publican; “as an heathen man and a publican”, Matthew 18:17.

Greek exairo (G1808) — to lift out, to put away; “Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person”, 1 Corinthians 5:13.

Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to examine, to prove; “let a man examine himself”, 1 Corinthians 11:28.

Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend as a shepherd, to feed; “to feed the church of God”, Acts 20:28.

Usage

"“tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — Bern claiming discipline for its council, 1559."

"“let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread” (1Co 11:28) — the Lausanne ministers on admission to the Supper."

"“to feed the church of God” (Act 20:28) — Viret and Beza expelled, and Geneva's academy furnished."
